title: new And delete
body:
`new` is used to alocate

```c++
int *p = new int;        // one int on the heap
int *a = new int[n];     // n of them, and n can come from cin
```

`new` asks for memory at **run time** and returns its [[Address|address]], so the
result always goes into a [[Pointer]]. `delete` hands it back.

```c++
delete p;        // for new
delete[] a;      // for new[]  -- the brackets are not optional
p = NULL;        // so a stale pointer is obviously stale
```

**Every `new` needs exactly one matching `delete`, and `new[]` needs `delete[]`.** Mismatching
them is undefined behaviour, and it is one of the four ways to get this wrong:

| Mistake | What you get |
|---|---|
| Forgetting `delete` | memory leak, grows until the program ends |
| `delete` twice | heap corruption, usually a crash later and elsewhere |
| Using the pointer after `delete` | dangling pointer, reads garbage |
| `delete` on a stack address | crash |

None of them is a [[Compile Errors|compile error]]. They are [[Runtime Errors]] at best and
[[Logic Errors]] at worst, and the crash usually happens nowhere near the bug.

This is the ability [[Static Allocation]] does not have: `int a[n]` with `n` from input is a
compile error, `new int[n]` is fine, because by then the program is running and `n` has a
value. That one difference is what makes [[Dynamic Arrays]] possible, and what makes a
[[Node]] allocated per insertion possible, which is the entire basis of the [[Linked List]].

Where the memory comes from is the heap, not the stack; see [[Stack and Heap]] for why those
are different regions with different rules. [[Dynamic Allocation]] · [[Variable Lifetime]]
